campaigns.title: A symbol is chunked once, as a whole

mutants.old: return [name for name in symbols if "." not in name]
mutants.breaks: a parser listing a method before its class consumes the method's text first, so the whole class is skipped

retired.reason: FR-1 is no longer 'a symbol is chunked once, as a whole'. The 2026-08-26 design gives that number to 'visibility is a value'; the old claim is replaced by FR-8 and FR-12, under which a chunk may hold several whole units and a signature is deliberately in two layers.

campaigns.title: An oversized symbol splits rather than truncating

mutants.breaks: only the first slice of a long function is indexed and the rest is lost silently

retired.reason: FR-3 is no longer 'an oversized symbol splits rather than truncating'. That claim moved to FR-10 and was demoted to a last resort behind FR-8, which splits on nested symbols first. FR-3 now means TypeScript's export-versus-accessibility rule.

campaigns.title: An unreadable file is still indexed

mutants.breaks: a file whose parser raises vanishes from the index with no signal

rekeyed.reason: Re-keyed 2026-08-26. The claim survives verbatim; only its number moved. `FR-4` now means 'Go has no private' and this campaign proves 'an unreadable file is still indexed', which the 2026-08-26 design calls `FR-16`. Left as `FR-4` the nightly would report a green claim nobody makes -- the same defect that retired `FR-1` and `FR-3`.

mutants.breaks: imports and the module docstring never reach the index

rekeyed.reason: Re-keyed 2026-08-26. Same claim, new number: `FR-5` now means 'a symbol yields its description'. Found when SF-02's FR-5 campaign landed and the runner reported SEVEN mutants under one requirement -- six new and one that had nothing to do with them.

campaigns.title: Visibility is a value, and each language's default is its own

mutants.breaks: Go's only visibility signal. Capitalisation is the whole rule, and without it every unexported identifier claims to be part of the package's interface

the container rule. An interface member carries no modifier and is implicitly public by the JLS; reading it as hidden dropped every interface method from the public set, which is how the defect shipped
the one column that separates `__init__` from `__checksum`. Collapsing them put a name-mangled member into the `exposes:` list of every generated `context.yaml`
Rust's third level. `pub(crate)` is module-scoped, and calling it public offers a crate-internal API to consumers outside the crate

campaigns.title: The filter returns the levels asked for, and cannot fail open

mutants.breaks: the defect this requirement closed, restored exactly: a request for `private` returns the whole file. One of the two live callers passes whatever an agent typed, so failing open is the worst direction for a filter whose job is to withhold

mutants.old: matched = "public" in requested if level == "unknown" else level in requested
mutants.breaks: the opposite failure, and the one that gets a gate switched off: every filtered request answers with silence, which reads as *this code does not exist* rather than as a broken filter

mutants.old: matched = "public" in requested if level == "unknown" else level in requested
mutants.breaks: `AD-5`. SQL and markdown have no access concept and report `unknown`, so treating it as a level nobody requests empties the index for two of the eight target languages

campaigns.title: A description is what was written above THIS declaration, and nothing else

mutants.breaks: attachment. `prev_sibling` alone finds a comment three blank lines above, so without the gap check every file's licence header becomes the description of its first declaration -- and every test about a PRESENT description still passes, which is why this mutant is the one that matters
stacked doc blocks. `///` and `//` lines arrive one node each, so taking only the nearest returns a doc block's last line and gives no sign the rest was dropped

mutants.old: while node.parent is not None and node.parent.start_point[0] == node.start_point[0]:
mutants.breaks: every documented TYPE in TypeScript and Go, whose comment precedes a wrapper -- an `export_statement` and a `type_declaration` -- rather than the declaration itself. A fixed per-language depth passed every method-level test and failed four of eight type-level ones

mutants.old: while node.parent is not None and node.parent.start_point[0] == node.start_point[0]:
mutants.breaks: the opposite: climbing past the declaration to the file itself, so one comment somewhere near the top becomes the description of everything in it
the description's text. `/**`, `///` and `#` appear in every doc in a language, so they carry no signal and make same-language chunks look alike to an embedding
Python's descriptions entirely. It is the one language whose description is not a comment, so no sibling walk substitutes for this

campaigns.title: A signature is the declaration without its body, behind its description

mutants.breaks: the whole point: a skeleton chunk carrying the full implementation is the body chunk again, and the two layers stop being distinguishable

mutants.old: return f"{doc}\n{signature}" if doc else signature
mutants.breaks: `FR-6`'s other half. A signature without its description is the thing `extract_symbol` already returned, and the reason this accessor exists is that a name and a shape retrieve worse than a name, a shape and a sentence
SQL. The declarative tier has no target block, so `extract_symbol_body` raises there -- and this is called once per symbol during a whole-repository scan, where one raise takes the scan down

campaigns.title: A qualified SQL object is one symbol, not one per name part

mutants.breaks: the defect exactly as it shipped: an `object_reference` holds one identifier per name part, so `public.orders` reports as TWO symbols and the index gains a chunk named after a schema. A test asserting `'public.orders' in symbols` would pass with both fragments still present, which is why the assertions are on the exact list

strict resolution `[agreed 2026-08-26]`. `orders` would resolve to `public.orders`, which is the bare-name matching that gives the knowledge graph its measured 48% ghost rate -- a name that looks unique is not the same as the right target. Re-pointed here on 2026-08-26: the first version aimed at a type guard in the SQL parser that turned out to be EQUIVALENT, because the query can only produce that node type. Strictness was never in the branch it named
